EN1.ti: 次の英文を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
EN1.c:
Most of us try hard to avoid failure. (1) [[u:It is often not failure itself that we fear, but how others see us when we fail.]] As a result, many people choose easy tasks that they are sure to complete, rather than difficult ones from which they could learn more.

However, some educators argue that we should (2) [[u:treat failure as information]]. When an experiment does not work, a scientist does not decide that she is a bad scientist. Instead, she sees the result as a sign of what to try next.

In one study, students who were taught to think of mistakes as part of learning worked longer on difficult problems than students who were not, and in the end they achieved higher scores. The lesson is clear: if we can stop worrying about how we look, failure can become one of our best teachers.

SS-RD-FORGET.ti: 次の英文（“Why We Forget”）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
SS-RD-FORGET.c:
Most people regard forgetting as a weakness, a sign that the brain is not working as well as it should. (1) [[u:Yet a growing number of researchers argue that forgetting is not so much a failure of memory as a necessary part of it.]] Every day we take in far more information than we could ever use, and if the brain kept all of it, finding what really matters would become extremely difficult.

Consider what happens when you move to a new house. For the first few weeks, you may find yourself walking toward the place where the light switch used to be. (2) [[u:Only when the old habit fades does the new one become automatic.]] In this sense, forgetting clears space so that more useful knowledge can take its place.

This does not mean that all forgetting is good. Losing the memory of a friend's name or an important appointment can cause real trouble. (3) [[u:What matters is not whether we forget, but what we forget.]] A healthy memory, researchers suggest, is one that keeps what is likely to be useful and lets go of the rest.

(4) [[u:Seen in this light, the occasional lapse of memory that worries so many of us may be less a symptom of decline than evidence that the brain is doing its job.]]

SS-RD-NAVI.ti: 次の英文（“Finding Our Way”）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
SS-RD-NAVI.c:
Not long ago, finding your way in an unfamiliar city meant studying a paper map, asking strangers for directions, and occasionally getting lost. Today, a smartphone tells us exactly where to turn. (1) [[u:Few would deny that this has made travel easier, but some researchers wonder what we have lost in exchange.]]

When we follow a paper map, we have to connect the picture in our hands to the streets around us. We notice a church on the corner or the shape of a park, and gradually we build a mental picture of the area. (2) [[u:A voice that tells us when to turn left or right requires no such effort, and as a result we may arrive at our destination with little idea of where we have been.]]

(3) [[u:This is not to say that we should throw away our phones.]] Rather, the point is that tools which do our thinking for us can also take away chances to develop our own abilities. (4) [[u:It is one thing to use a tool; it is quite another to depend on it so completely that we cannot manage without it.]]

SS-RD-READ.ti: 次の英文（“Reading Slowly in a Fast World”）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
SS-RD-READ.c:
We read more words today than ever before: messages, news headlines, posts, and comments, one after another. (1) [[u:But reading more is not the same as reading well, and there are signs that the habit of skimming is changing the way we approach longer texts.]]

When we read on a screen, we tend to jump from one line to another, looking for key words. This is useful when we only need a piece of information. (2) [[u:The trouble is that we may come to read everything in this way, including texts that ask us to follow a long argument or to imagine another person's feelings.]]

Deep reading is slow by nature. It requires us to keep earlier sentences in mind, to question what the writer is saying, and to connect it with what we already know. (3) [[u:None of this can be done in a hurry.]]

(4) [[u:It is not that we have lost the ability to read deeply, but that we are given fewer and fewer occasions to use it.]] Like a muscle, the ability weakens when it is not used.

SS-RD-SILENCE.ti: 次の英文（“The Meaning of Silence”）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
SS-RD-SILENCE.c:
In many conversations, a pause of even a few seconds can make people uncomfortable. Someone quickly says something, anything, to fill the gap. (1) [[u:It is as if silence were an empty space that must be filled before it becomes embarrassing.]]

However, silence is not always empty. In some cultures, a short pause before answering shows that the listener is taking the question seriously. (2) [[u:To reply too quickly may even suggest that one has not thought about what the other person said.]] When people from such different backgrounds talk to each other, a pause that one person intends as respect can be taken by the other as a lack of interest.

(3) [[u:Misunderstandings of this kind are hard to notice, because neither speaker is aware that the other is following different rules.]] Each simply concludes that the other person is rude or unfriendly.

The solution is not to decide which rule is correct. It is to recognize that the meaning of silence, like the meaning of words, depends on the people who share it. (4) [[u:The more we are aware of this, the less likely we are to judge others by standards they never agreed to.]]

SS-RD-VEG.ti: 次の英文（“Judging Food by Its Looks”）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
SS-RD-VEG.c:
Walk into any supermarket and you will see rows of vegetables that look almost identical: carrots of the same length, tomatoes of the same bright red. (1) [[u:What you will not see are the many vegetables that never reached the shelves simply because they did not look right.]]

Farmers know that stores are unwilling to buy vegetables with unusual shapes or small marks, even when they taste exactly the same. As a result, a considerable amount of perfectly good food is thrown away before it leaves the farm. (2) [[u:It is not the quality of the food that decides its fate, but its appearance.]]

Some shops have begun to sell such vegetables at lower prices, and many customers have been happy to buy them. (3) [[u:This suggests that the demand for perfect-looking food may have been created as much by the stores as by the shoppers themselves.]]

(4) [[u:Had we been willing to accept vegetables as they are, much of this waste could have been avoided.]] The question we should ask is not how vegetables look, but whether we are wasting what the earth has produced.
